USA.mechanism: A complaint handled inside an institution instead of by the police runs down the legal clock, and once a state's deadline for charging or suing has passed, the delay has become permanent protection.
USA.story:
In 1974 the Catholic bishop of Lafayette, Louisiana, appointed Fr Gilbert Gauthe chaplain to a Boy Scout troop. Allegations that Gauthe had abused altar boys had already reached the diocese. He was sent for therapy in 1976 and put back to work, and he later admitted abusing 37 children between 1972 and 1983. He pleaded guilty in October 1985 and was sentenced to 20 years, and the diocese paid out more than $20 million.

The decision that mattered was taken in 1974: the complaint was treated as a staffing problem. The same choice was made elsewhere. In Stockton, California, Bishop Roger Mahony knew of concerns about Fr Oliver O'Grady by 1980; after police declined to charge him in 1984, Mahony moved him to another parish and later made him pastor. O'Grady was convicted in 1993.

Keeping a complaint in-house has a particular consequence in the United States, because every state sets a deadline, a statute of limitations, after which a crime can no longer be charged and a survivor can no longer sue. Most people abused as children say so decades later, so the deadline usually runs out first. A Pennsylvania grand jury reporting in 2018 identified 301 priests and at least 1,000 child victims in six dioceses over about 70 years, found that bishops "went to great lengths to keep it secret" and had moved abusers, and recorded that most of the crimes were by then too old to prosecute. Secrecy had not merely delayed those cases; it had ended them.

So the deadlines themselves became the fight. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million lobbying in eight northeastern states between 2011 and 2018; in Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the state Catholic Conference spent over $7.6 million and the insurance federation nearly $20.7 million between 2014 and 2024. Where deadlines did fall, institutions filed for bankruptcy, which halts lawsuits and settles every claim at once out of whatever assets a court recognises. At least 41 dioceses and religious orders did so, along with the Boy Scouts and USA Gymnastics, several within hours or days of a trial, a deposition or a new law. In Milwaukee, $57 million had been moved into a cemetery trust, where claimants could not reach it.

Money bought the same delay without a clock. Jeffrey Epstein was reported to the FBI in 1996 with no known action, and in 2007, after a Palm Beach police investigation, a federal non-prosecution agreement closed the federal case; he served 13 months on a state plea, and federal sex-trafficking charges came only in July 2019.

The American record is mostly what grand juries, reporters and lawsuits dug out years after the fact, because the bodies that heard the first complaints did not pass them on. When a case surfaces here, the questions that decide it are who was told first, in what year, and whether the law in that state still permits anything to be done.

PHL.mechanism: Enforcement aimed at a place moves the trade to another place, and once the places were closed it moved onto a webcam paid for from abroad.
PHL.story:
Shutting a red-light district rarely ends the trade inside it. It moves it, because the buyers and the people selling children to them are still there the next morning. In 1992 Manila's mayor, Alfredo Lim, closed the Ermita district, where the city's sex industry had been concentrated. The businesses reopened north of the city in Angeles City, a town that had grown up around the US Clark Air Base and had just lost it, the base closing the same year, which left bars with no customers and a new clientele of foreign visitors. Thirty-three years later the US government's trafficking report still lists Angeles City, along with Boracay, Olongapo, Puerto Galera and Surigao, among the places where children are sold. That is the measure of what the 1992 closure achieved: it changed the address.

The second move was out of any address at all. Police pressure on bars and streets worked on its own terms, and the charity International Justice Mission measured a fall of 79 to 86 per cent in establishment-based child sex trafficking in the cities it targeted between 2006 and 2016. Across almost the same years, from 2014 to 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for child sexual exploitation rose more than twelvefold. In the new arrangement a buyer abroad pays an adult the child lives with or knows, and directs the abuse over a video call as it happens. Nobody crosses a border and nothing is smuggled. One Australian man did this over Skype for nearly five years, paying the children's mother; they were two and seven when it began. International Justice Mission estimates that one in every 100 Filipino children was a victim of online sexual exploitation in 2022, and in its 2020 study the median victim was 11 and 9 per cent were three or younger.

With nothing physical moving, the trail is the money and the chat, and both sit abroad. Australia's financial regulator alleged that Westpac had breached anti-money-laundering law more than 23 million times, including failing to check transactions associated with possible child exploitation, and in September 2020 the bank agreed a A$1.3 billion penalty. In June 2024, 32 investigators at Europol worked through more than 10 million lines of messages between about 12,000 customer accounts and 100 seller accounts, built up over twelve years, and produced leads on 197 buyers for authorities in 24 countries. In 2017, 64 per cent of the cases taken up by the Philippine anti-trafficking unit began as a referral from a foreign police force, which is what it looks like when the evidence of a crime committed in one country sits on a server and in a bank account in another.

The Philippines shows that enforcement aimed at a location relocates the trade, and that its final location has no address. The paying customers, their banks and the police who can read their records are mostly in wealthy countries, so when a case here is reported, ask which country the buyer was in and what was done to him there.

CHL.mechanism: An abuser who is useful to powerful people is protected by them, and when the state itself is holding children, that protection extends to the state's own institutions.
CHL.story:
Authorities in Siegburg, West Germany, issued a warrant in 1959 for Paul Schäfer, a former Nazi army corporal, for abusing two boys. He left the country and in January 1961 settled in southern Chile with a small group of followers, founding a commune called Colonia Dignidad. It ran a free school and clinic and took in children from local farms. In 1966 a teenager who escaped reached the West German embassy and asked for help. The embassy sent a delegation, reported that it found no evidence, and German diplomats went on describing the place as a model colony. Chilean politicians dismissed other escapees' accounts in the 1960s; the colony had ties to the men preparing the 1973 coup. Chilean officials believe the dictatorship's secret police used it from 1973 as a site for torturing opponents, and Schäfer was charged with aiding the regime. An investigation into the abuse opened only after Chilean mothers complained in 1997.

Schäfer had already gone. He hid in Argentina until he was found in March 2005, and in May 2006 a Chilean court sentenced him to 20 years for sexually abusing 25 children. Germany's foreign minister said in April 2016 that over many years German diplomats had "at best looked away".

Rank inside the church did the same work. Parishioners reported Fr Fernando Karadima to the Archbishop of Santiago in 1984; a church investigation in 2004 and 2005 found the complaints credible and Cardinal Errázuriz shelved it. The Vatican found Karadima guilty in 2011 and ordered him to a life of prayer and penance, a church penalty that carries no criminal consequence and no public record. Four of his protégés had become bishops, and one of them, Juan Barros, was made bishop of Osorno in 2015. After a 2,300-page report by Archbishop Charles Scicluna, Pope Francis wrote in April 2018 that he had been mistaken about Chile, and in May every Chilean bishop offered to resign. In July 2019 Chile removed the time limit on prosecuting child sexual abuse.

The state's own institutions were protected the same way. Babies were taken from mainly poor mothers, some told their child had died, and sent for adoption abroad, most heavily under the Pinochet dictatorship; a judge opened a criminal investigation in 2018 into about 8,000 adoptions between 1970 and 1999, a congressional committee concluded the state was responsible, and as of September 2023 nobody had been brought to justice. Family-court judges who interviewed children in state-funded residential homes in 2012 found sexual abuse was constant, and in one home in Arica a network organised by the carers, with 24 girls leaving the home and returning drugged at dawn. Their report was held back until a news organisation printed it in July 2013, after which the government intervened in 34 homes.

Protection here looks less like a conspiracy than like officials who had a use for an institution and therefore took its word: an embassy that inspected a commune and found nothing, a cardinal who filed a credible report away. When a closed community or a state institution holds children, ask who had the right to inspect it, what they wrote, and who decided whether anyone would read it.

ROU.mechanism: A country that keeps very large numbers of children in state institutions holds a standing supply, and whoever is buying draws on it: adoption agencies in the 1990s, traffickers afterwards.
ROU.story:
Romania's Decree 770, passed in 1966, banned abortion. Many of the children born in the years that followed were left in state orphanages and in institutions for disabled children, where they were neglected, sedated and physically and sexually abused; at the Siret children's psychiatric hospital such abuse was reported to be common. When Ceaușescu fell in 1989 and television showed roughly 100,000 children living in these places, foreign families arrived to adopt.

What happened next was shaped by how the adoptions were paid for. Private agencies charged between €7,500 and €25,000 for a placement, and the system, in the words of the German broadcaster DW, "quickly became awash in corruption". A fee for each completed adoption pays an intermediary for producing a child, not for establishing that the child needed one, and the people who could produce children were the staff of institutions and the people who dealt with poor mothers. Romania put adoptions on hold in July 1990, halted them in June 1991 and outlawed baby selling that August. A government commission found in 2001 that money had been siphoned off by middlemen and officials; 458 intercountry adoptions still went through in 2002 and 332 in 2003. In June 2004, under pressure from the European Union, a law banned foreign adoption except by grandparents, and Romania's own returns show 2 in 2005 and none in 2006. Between 1994 and 2008, 5,285 Romanian children had been adopted into the United States alone.

The route closed; the supply did not. The 2025 US trafficking report says children in government-run institutions, particularly girls in homes for people with disabilities, are at risk of sex trafficking, and that alleged complicity, misconduct and negligence by government employees in those cases remains a concern. Traffickers reach the same children by a method called the "loverboy": a man presents himself as a boyfriend to a girl who has no family behind her, and then sells her, which is quieter than force because she travels willingly. In September 2020 Romanian and British investigators working as a joint team arrested 21 members of a group running since 2009 that exploited girls in prostitution inside Romania while they were minors and moved them to the UK, Ireland and Germany once they turned 18. Romanian courts convicted 161 traffickers in 2024, 143 for sex trafficking, and 600 victims were identified.

Romania is also one of the places where abuse images are stored: the Internet Watch Foundation had 21,188 web addresses hosted there taken down in 2025, 7 per cent of its total. Hosting counts record where companies keep servers rather than where children were harmed.

The children most easily taken are the ones the state is already holding, and closing one route to them changes who comes for them next, not whether anyone does. So when a country bans or reforms foreign adoption, the question is not whether the ban held, but whether anyone is now watching the children in its own care homes.

CAF.mechanism: Soldiers sent to protect children can be tried only by the country that sent them, so the strongest sanction the mission has is a plane ticket home.
CAF.story:
At the camp for displaced people beside Bangui's M'Poko airport, between December 2013 and June 2014, six boys aged 9 to 13 told UN staff that French soldiers had sexually abused them in return for food rations. The soldiers belonged to Operation Sangaris, a French force in the Central African Republic under its own command rather than the UN's. The boys were living where armed adults decided what there was to eat, which is the condition the exchange rested on.

The UN did not pass its internal record of those interviews to the French authorities. A UN official, Anders Kompass, handed it over himself; he was suspended and resigned in 2016. Paris prosecutors had opened a preliminary inquiry in July 2014, which grew to cover accusations by fifteen children. In January 2018 French investigating judges dismissed the case, a decision called a non-lieu, meaning they judged the evidence insufficient to put anyone on trial, citing inconsistencies in the children's accounts. The prosecutor said it could not be affirmed at the end of the investigation that no sexual abuse had been committed. No soldier was charged.

The UN peacekeepers who came later were covered by a different rule with a similar result. Countries lend troops to a UN mission on condition that their own courts keep jurisdiction over them, so the UN can investigate a soldier but cannot prosecute him; it can send him home. In Dékoa, two recorded allegations against personnel from Gabon and Burundi led to interviews with some 136 alleged victims, 48 per cent of all victims the UN recorded worldwide in 2016. Press accounts reported that at least 98 girls described abuse and that 41 troops were identified and sent home without charges. Human Rights Watch documented eight cases in Bambari in January 2016, including a 14-year-old girl who said she was gang-raped near the airport, most in the months when a Republic of Congo contingent guarded it. UN tables list 17 allegations against soldiers from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with 15 child victims; that battalion withdrew in January 2016. In September 2021 all Gabonese units, about 450 personnel, were repatriated after further allegations, and Gabon opened an investigation.

The armed groups the mission was there to contain take children directly. In 2024 UN monitors verified sexual violence against 114 girls in the country: 58 by armed groups of the CPC coalition, 35 by government and pro-government forces, including 21 by the national defence forces and 9 by the Wagner-linked Azande group, 11 by the PRNC and 2 by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces. They verified the abduction of 141 children, most for recruitment, sexual violence, or both.

This is what happens when the only authority present has no power to punish. "Repatriated" describes travel, not justice, and it is where most of these cases end. When a unit is sent home, look for a named court in its own country and a date.

HTI.mechanism: After a disaster, outsiders arrive with money, food and transport, and each of them answers to a body somewhere else rather than to Haiti.
HTI.story:
Sri Lankan soldiers served in Haiti from 2004 to 2007 as part of the UN peacekeeping mission. The UN's own internal oversight office concluded afterwards that sexual exploitation and abuse of children by members of the contingent "were frequent and occurred usually at night, and at virtually every location where the contingent personnel were deployed", and said the charges should include statutory rape, meaning sex with a child below the age at which the law recognises consent. An Associated Press investigation in 2017 found that at least 134 of the soldiers had exploited at least nine children in a sex ring.

What happened to them is set by the terms on which countries lend troops to the UN: a peacekeeper can be tried only by his own country's courts. The UN's power stops at sending him home. In November 2007, 114 of the 950-strong contingent were accused and 108 were sent back, three of them officers. Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts consensual. Nobody was jailed, and in 2016 one victim received a single payment made as a gesture rather than as compensation ordered by any court.

The 2010 earthquake brought a second kind of outsider. Oxfam GB's own investigation in 2011 found that its staff in Haiti had used prostitutes, some alleged to be underage. Staff including the country director were allowed to resign, which closes an employer's inquiry and leaves nothing a future employer would see. The British charity regulator found in 2019 that Oxfam had not pursued all lines of enquiry about minors, had not adequately investigated an email of 18 July 2011 alleging that its employees were sexually abusing minors, and had reported none of it to the regulator or the police; by 2019 it was no longer possible to establish whether minors had been involved.

The third kind arrived to take children away. On 29 January 2010 ten American Baptist missionaries were stopped trying to move 33 children to the Dominican Republic without documentation; the kidnapping charges were dropped and the organiser, Laura Silsby, was convicted only of arranging illegal travel and sentenced to the time she had already served. In 2007 a Haitian centre had been forced to return 47 children it was holding for international adoption, after misleading their parents with payments and keeping them in conditions the International Organization for Migration called inhumane. Between 2003 and 2022, 13,986 Haitian children were sent abroad for adoption. The charity Lumos traced about $70 million of orphanage funding between 2010 and 2017 and found 92 per cent of funders were based in the United States and 90 per cent were faith-based, and that the donations themselves cause orphanages to be founded, some purely for profit, which then recruit children from families who still have them.

Haiti shows that a disaster creates demand for children at the same moment it strips the country of the ability to ask questions, and that each group of outsiders is accountable to a court, a regulator or a church board thousands of miles away. When money flows to an orphanage, the question is not how well the building is run but whether the children in it have parents.

ARG.mechanism: A state that took the babies of the people it was disappearing, and locked the theft in place by registering each child as somebody else's, so that the crime outlived the regime in the form of adults who did not know who they were.
ARG.story:
A boy was born on 17 April 1977 inside a secret detention centre called La Escuelita, in Bahía Blanca, after his parents were kidnapped in Cutral Có, Neuquén. Under Argentina's military government, which ruled from 1976 to 1983, babies born to detained or disappeared mothers were handed to military families and allies of the regime and registered on paper as their biological children.

That registration is what made the practice work. A falsified birth record does not merely hide a child; it removes the document that any later search would start from, so there is nothing to follow back from the adoptive family to the mother. Most of the children grew up not knowing they had been adopted at all. The Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo, formed in 1977 to find children kidnapped alongside their disappeared parents or born to mothers in detention, and whose work led to the creation of Argentina's National Bank of Genetic Data, which holds DNA from the searching families, because once the paperwork is false, biology is the only remaining link. The man born in Bahía Blanca was identified in July 2025. He was the 140th found, out of about 500 children taken; the Grandmothers had found 97 by 2008 and 133 by July 2023.

The courts reached the policy itself only decades later. On 5 July 2012 a federal tribunal in Buenos Aires found that the junta had operated a systematic plan to take these children, covering roughly 31 to 35 abductions in that trial. The former dictator Jorge Videla was sentenced to 50 years and the last dictator, Reynaldo Bignone, to 15, with nine other defendants receiving 15 to 40 years.

Uruguay shows what blocks such a case. A pregnant 19-year-old Argentine, detained in Buenos Aires in August 1976, was moved secretly to Montevideo, gave birth in a military hospital and had her baby taken in December 1976 and left with a police officer's family, who raised her under another identity for 23 years. The investigation was closed in 2003 under Uruguay's 1986 Expiry Law, an amnesty that barred prosecutions for the dictatorship's crimes. In February 2011 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights found Uruguay responsible and ruled the amnesty legally ineffective, which reopened the ground for charges.

Argentina also shows how police protection sustains ordinary trafficking. Marita Verón, aged 23, disappeared in Tucumán in 2002, allegedly taken into forced prostitution; lawyers for her family said police were often paid to protect brothel rings. In December 2012 a Tucumán court acquitted all 13 defendants, which brought national protests, and in December 2013 the province's Supreme Court reversed the acquittals and found 10 of them guilty.

The useful thing to carry from Argentina is that the hardest part of taking a child is not the taking but the paperwork, and that documents are also what undoes it: a genetic database, a court ruling that struck down an amnesty. When a state is accused of taking children, ask who holds the birth records, and whether anyone is legally permitted to open them.

NOR.mechanism: A receiving country is part of the supply: steady demand, backed by its diplomats, kept children moving after the sending country tried to stop.
NOR.story:
In 1974 and 1975 South Korea tried to reduce the number of children it sent abroad for adoption. Scandinavian diplomats pressed it to keep sending them. That is the part of intercountry adoption least often described, because the arrangement is usually explained as rescue: on this side of it, the children were asked for.

Norway received 6,295 Korean children between 1955 and 2008, part of about 163,898 sent abroad from South Korea in those years. What the demand did at the Korean end was set out by that country's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, a state body with the power to investigate past abuses, which reported on 26 March 2025 after examining petitions from 367 adoptees sent to 11 countries between 1964 and 1999. It found human rights violations in at least 56 of those cases. Agencies had sent a set number of children each month to meet the demand of foreign agencies, which inverts the process: instead of a child being found to need a family, a quota had to be filled, and the paperwork was made to fit. Children with known, living parents were registered as orphans, consent was not properly obtained, adoptive parents were not vetted, and when a child died before departure another child was sent under that child's identity. The commission said the Korean state had treated sending children abroad as a cheap substitute for welfare at home. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.

Norway began examining its own side in 2023, opening an investigation into whether illegal or unethical practices occurred in its intercountry adoptions and whether Norwegian officials failed to control them. The foreign ministry said in 2024 that it was aware of serious findings. In September 2025 a Korean-born adoptee served notice of a lawsuit against the Norwegian state alleging that her adoption had been illegal, a claim that has not been tested in court.

One other Norwegian thread is on this map, and it is not an abuse case. After the US Justice Department released documents about Jeffrey Epstein in 2026, Norway's economic-crime agency investigated the former prime minister and Council of Europe secretary-general Thorbjørn Jagland over whether gifts, travel and loans were received in connection with his position. His lawyers said on 12 February 2026 that he had been charged with aggravated corruption, and his home and two other properties were searched. He denies all charges. It is recorded here for the reach of Epstein's contacts into politics, not as an allegation about children.

Norway is a country where no abuse happened on its soil and which still appears on this map, because demand and the diplomacy behind it were inputs to the system. When a country adopted thousands of children from abroad, the question for it is not whether its families meant well, but whether it ever checked how the children were obtained, and what it did when a sending country tried to stop.

BLR.mechanism: Two kinds of traffic: abuse sold as a paid subscription, which leaves a trail of named customers, and children moved across a border in wartime under a label that creates no record at all.
BLR.story:
In a Paris hotel on 30 July 2003, US agents arrested two men from Minsk: Yahor Zalatarou, the president of a company called Regpay, and Alexei Buchnev, its marketing director. The next day Regpay's technical administrator, Aliaksandr Boika, was arrested in Tarragona, Spain. Regpay processed paid memberships for about 50 websites, including child abuse sites it ran itself, serving thousands of subscribers around the world. Customers paid by credit card, the payments were routed through banks in Latvia, and a Florida firm called Connections laundered the proceeds.

Running abuse as a subscription business is what made the case reach so far. A paying customer has to identify himself to his bank, so the business's own accounts are a list of names and addresses, which is why hundreds of subscribers were arrested in the United States and other countries after the company was seized. The US attorney general announced the case in January 2004. All three men pleaded guilty in New Jersey: Buchnev was sentenced to 40 months in May 2006, and Zalatarou and Boika to 25 years each on 9 August 2006. The chief executive of Connections pleaded guilty to money laundering.

The second traffic runs the other way, and leaves no accounts to seize. After Russia's full invasion of Ukraine in 2022, about 2,100 children from occupied Ukraine were brought to Belarus. In July 2023 the head of the Belarus Red Cross said they had come for "health improvement" and that this would continue. A health trip is a description, not a legal process: there is no register of names, no return date and no court involved, which is precisely what distinguishes it from an evacuation. On the Russian side the paperwork went further. A decree of 30 May 2022 eased Russian citizenship for Ukrainian children so they could be adopted by Russian families, a register of willing families was created, and families were paid for each adopted child granted citizenship. On 17 March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and Russia's children's commissioner, Maria Lvova-Belova, for the war crimes of unlawful deportation and unlawful transfer of children. Both are charged; neither has been tried.

The same method was prosecuted once before. Nazi Germany seized children in occupied Poland and elsewhere who were judged racially valuable, held them in homes and placed them with German families under new identities; Deutsche Welle reports estimates of up to 200,000 Polish children kidnapped and forcibly made German. At Nuremberg, 14 officials of the SS office responsible were tried, and on 10 March 1948 the tribunal convicted 13 and acquitted one.

What links the two halves of this record is bookkeeping. One business kept records because it needed to be paid, and those records convicted its customers; the other movement of children was arranged so that no record would exist. When children are taken out of a war zone, ask who wrote down their names, who holds that list, and what document says they are coming back.

SYR.mechanism: War reaches the same children twice: organised capture and sale inside the country, then, outside it, refugee families with no legal standing and nobody to complain to.
SYR.story:
Islamic State fighters attacked Sinjar, in northern Iraq, on 3 August 2014 and took thousands of Yazidi captives. They were moved in buses and trucks to holding sites at Tal Afar, Mosul and Baaj, and women and girls were then taken on to Raqqa in Syria. The organisation is the thing to notice: transport, holding sites, and a market at the end of it, run as a system rather than as separate attacks. In June 2016 the UN commission of inquiry on Syria found that Islamic State had committed genocide, that women and girls, some as young as nine, were sold at market and held in sexual slavery, and that boys were put into training camps. At that point more than 3,200 Yazidi women and children were still held, mostly in Syria, and thousands remain missing.

Outside Syria the same children lost a different kind of protection. A refugee has no right to work in most host countries and often no documents, which means no employer to answer to, no landlord's record and little prospect that a complaint to the police will go anywhere. In the Maameltein district of Jounieh, in Lebanon, security forces freed as many as 75 Syrian women from two brothels in March 2016 and more than a dozen people were charged with sex trafficking; the same premises had been raided in 2011, when a 17-year-old Syrian girl was found inside, and had reopened after about three months. Human Rights Watch said Syrian refugee women were at particular risk.

In Türkiye, which has hosted about 2.9 million displaced Syrians, the 2025 US trafficking report says Syrian girls are forced into marriages in unofficial religious ceremonies, particularly in poor rural areas, and then subjected to domestic servitude and sex trafficking. An unofficial ceremony leaves no registration, which means no age check at the time and no record of the girl afterwards. In Jordan, the same report says Syrian refugee women and girls have been sold into forced marriages, and that in 2022 the authorities investigated a mother for allegedly exploiting her two daughters with foreign tourists.

Inside Syria the counting continues and stays small. UN monitors verified the abduction of 14 children in 2024, five boys and nine girls, by the Patriotic Revolutionary Youth Movement, Syrian government forces and the Kurdish YPG and YPJ, most for recruitment. "Verified" means a monitor confirmed each case, which in a war means reaching the child or a witness, so the figure is a floor rather than an estimate.

Syria shows that displacement is itself a mechanism: it removes registration, legal status and a police force a family can approach, and those are the things that make a child hard to sell. When you read that refugee girls are being married off, ask who is legally allowed to register a marriage in that country, and who checks the age of a bride who has no papers.

DNK.mechanism: A democratic state removed children as policy, used charities to select them, and called it help; the same country's demand also paid for children taken abroad.
DNK.story:
In May 1951 Danish authorities, working with Save the Children Denmark, asked teachers and priests in Greenland, then a Danish colony, to pick out children aged six to ten. Twenty-two Inuit children were sent to foster families in Denmark to be brought up as "little Danes". Many of the families had not wanted to let them go.

The removal was presented as temporary and educational, and what happened next is why the distinction mattered less than it sounded. About eighteen months later 16 of the children were sent back to Greenland, but not to their parents: they were placed in a children's home built by the Danish Red Cross, and many never lived with their families again. Six were adopted in Denmark instead. A report in 2020 found that half of the 22 later had mental health problems. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen apologised in December 2020, and in March 2022, after the survivors took legal action, the six who were left were each awarded 250,000 kroner. The apology came seven decades after the fact; the money came only when they sued.

Denmark was also on the receiving side of the trade in children. Between 1965 and 2008, 9,297 South Korean children were sent to Denmark for adoption. South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2025 that agencies there had sent a set number of children each month to meet the demand of foreign agencies and had registered children with known, living parents as orphans, which shows what steady foreign demand does to a sending country's paperwork. Sri Lankan children were adopted into Denmark in the 1980s, during a period the sources call the baby-farm years. In March 2016 Denmark suspended adoptions from Ethiopia, where families had been given orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and where adoptions abroad had risen from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008 before Ethiopia banned them in 2018. In 2024 Denmark's only intercountry adoption agency said it was shutting down.

The Greenland experiment is a reminder that the people doing the selecting can be a government ministry and two of the best-known children's charities, and that nobody involved needed to think of it as harm. When a state says it is giving children a better life somewhere else, the questions are whether the families agreed, what document says the children are coming back, and who was still responsible for them once they had.

PAK.mechanism: A case can be ended before it begins, by a police station that declines to write the complaint down and a law that lets a family be paid to forgive.
PAK.story:
In the village of Hussain Khanwala, in Kasur district of Punjab, a local gang filmed the sexual abuse of at least 280 children between 2006 and 2014 and then used the recordings against the children's parents, threatening to release them. The film was both the crime and the means of silence: a parent who complained risked having the video of their own child published. Parents did go to the police, repeatedly, and the police did not act. Arrests came only in August 2015, after relatives clashed with the authorities on 8 August and the press took the story up. The Punjab law minister described the reports as a land dispute. Police and a local member of the provincial assembly, Malik Ahmad Saeed Khan, were alleged to have tried to cover the case up; those allegations were not verified for this record. In 2016 an anti-terrorism court in Lahore sentenced two men to life imprisonment, and 12 other accused men were acquitted.

Pakistan's religious schools show the same blockage with a legal mechanism added. There are more than 22,000 registered madrassas, Islamic seminaries, with at least 2 million pupils. An Associated Press investigation published on 21 November 2017 found that sexual abuse by clerics in them was widespread and seldom prosecuted, that police were often paid off and refused to register cases, and that families of poor victims were pressed to forgive the cleric and accept money. Pakistani law permits this: in certain offences the victim's side can pardon the accused, which converts a criminal prosecution into a private settlement that can be bought. In one case a teacher confessed to abusing a nine-year-old and walked free after the mother forgave him for $300. The religious affairs minister dismissed the claims. Police told the news agency that clerics are almost never convicted, and a follow-up investigation in 2020, based on dozens of police reports, found the pattern unchanged.

Girls are also sold out of the country. In 2018 and 2019 brokers sold 629 poor Pakistani girls and women, many of them Christian, to Chinese men as brides, the word "bride" doing the work of making a purchase look like a family arrangement.

The lesson here is about the first five minutes of a case, not the courtroom. A crime that is never written down does not exist in any statistic, and a pardon that can be purchased ends the ones that are. When a country reports very few convictions, ask how many complaints its police agreed to record.

BGD.mechanism: Statelessness removes the things that let a child or a parent complain, and the official figures measure the courts rather than the crime.
BGD.story:
More than one million Rohingya refugees live in 33 camps around Cox's Bazar, in south-eastern Bangladesh. They are there because of what a UN fact-finding mission documented across the border: hundreds of Rohingya women and girls raped by Myanmar's army during the 2017 clearance operations, with 80 per cent of the corroborated cases being gang rapes, and Rohingya men and boys, some as young as twelve, held at Buthidaung prison in 2012 and subjected to sexual violence.

In the camps a second exposure begins, and it works through what the refugees do not have. A Rohingya family in Bangladesh has no citizenship, no right to work and often no identity document, so there is no employer, no landlord and no legal standing behind a complaint, and the police force in the camps is itself described in the 2025 US trafficking report as corrupt. The same report says tourists near Cox's Bazar have increased the demand for commercial sex, including with Rohingya girls.

Bangladeshi girls are also taken abroad, to India, Pakistan and the Gulf states, and observers estimate that children make up 40 per cent of the Bangladeshis exploited in sex trafficking outside the country. The report names corruption and official complicity as significant concerns. It also records that courts convicted 103 traffickers in the latest year, down from 407 the year before. A conviction count moves for reasons that have nothing to do with how many children were harmed: how many cases police brought, how many prosecutors took on, how many judges reached a verdict. Read as a measure of safety, a fall like that points the wrong way.

An older route ran through adoption. A Dutch commission chaired by Tjibbe Joustra reported in February 2021, after a two-year investigation, that there had been serious violations in adoptions from several countries including Bangladesh between 1967 and the late 1990s, and that the Dutch government had failed for decades to prevent them; the government revealed that its officials had been aware of wrongdoing for years without intervening, and suspended all intercountry adoption with immediate effect on 8 February 2021.

What Bangladesh demonstrates is that protection is made of paperwork and standing, not of goodwill: the children most at risk here are the ones no state will claim. And when a country's trafficking convictions drop sharply in a single year, the thing to establish is whether fewer crimes were committed or fewer cases were taken up.

SOM.mechanism: Need is the lever: children came to the military bases for food and medicine, and the exchange happened there, while the group the bases were fighting took children by force.
SOM.story:
Near Baidoa, in southern Somalia, in May 2013, a 12-year-old girl was allegedly raped by a Ugandan soldier serving with the African Union Mission in Somalia, known as AMISOM, which had been sent to fight the armed group Al-Shabaab. Human Rights Watch published a report on 8 September 2014 based on 50 interviews, 21 of them with survivors. It documented 10 incidents of sexual abuse, including rape and sexual assault, and 14 cases of sexual exploitation by African Union soldiers, mainly Ugandan personnel at and around the force's headquarters and Burundian personnel at their base in Mogadishu. Four of the rape cases and one sexual assault involved girls under 18.

How the women and girls came to be there matters more than where. Many had gone to the bases to ask for medicine or aid, one of them for her sick baby; interpreters working for the force arranged the soldiers' access to them, and some were pressed into sex in exchange for money, food and medicine. This is what the term "sexual exploitation" covers, as distinct from assault: when a base holds the only medicine within reach, a soldier's demand is not an offer a mother is in a position to refuse, and nothing has to be done by force for the outcome to be the same.

The armed group on the other side takes children outright and in far greater numbers. In 2024 UN monitors verified the abduction of 887 children in Somalia, 850 of them by Al-Shabaab and mostly in order to make them fighters. They verified sexual violence against 267 children, 265 of them girls: 120 cases attributed to Al-Shabaab, 110 to unidentified attackers, 14 to government security forces, 11 of those to the Somali National Army, and 7 to Ethiopia's Liyu Police. The UN Secretary-General noted a fivefold increase in gang rapes.

Somalia puts two risks on the same child, and the second one is easy to miss because it looks like aid rather than attack. When a foreign force is protecting a place, it is worth knowing who controls the food and medicine there, and in which country its soldiers would have to be tried.

BFA.mechanism: When a government arms civilian auxiliaries to fight a war, its own side appears in the abduction figures, and the only body counting is a monitoring mission whose totals are a floor.
BFA.story:
In 2024 UN monitors verified the abduction of 309 children in Burkina Faso. The armed group JNIM took 157, the Islamic State affiliate known as ISGS took 80, unidentified attackers took 47, and 25 were taken by the state's own Defence and Security Forces and the Volunteers for the Defence of the Homeland, civilians recruited and armed by the government to fight alongside the army. The monitors also verified the rape of four girls that year, two of them by those volunteers. In 2022 they had verified the rape of 16 girls, two by the Defence and Security Forces.

Two things in that paragraph decide how it should be read. The first is the word verified: a UN monitor has to confirm each case, usually by reaching the child or a witness, in a country where armed groups control roads and whole districts. The figure is therefore a minimum, not an estimate of what happened. The second is who appears in the list. Arming volunteers gives a government fighters it does not have to train, pay or discipline like soldiers, and it also means the force a family would report an abduction to is sometimes the force that carried it out.

Children also cross Burkina Faso's borders for other reasons. The 2025 US trafficking report says highly organised Nigerian networks, some linked to Nigerian cult organisations, move women and girls to mining regions in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire, and it names corruption and official complicity, including among officials responsible for anti-trafficking work, as significant concerns. In 2019 Nigerian police raided a building in Kaduna presented as an Islamic school and freed more than 300 captives; they said some had been brought from Burkina Faso, Mali and Ghana.

Nothing at all is measured outside the war. There is no representative survey of technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation anywhere in West and Central Africa, so abuse that does not pass in front of a UN monitor does not enter the record.

Burkina Faso is a case where the count and the accused come from the same place. A number that had to be verified in a war zone is a floor on the real figure, and when a state's own auxiliaries are on the list of abductors, the practical question is which authority is in a position to investigate them.

GMB.mechanism: A law aimed at the licensed, inspectable part of the trade moves the rest of it into private houses, while the buyers remain citizens of other countries.
GMB.story:
The Senegambia Strip, the main tourist area on The Gambia's coast, brings in European visitors by the planeload. The 2025 US trafficking report says some of them, primarily from the United Kingdom, reportedly travel there to exploit children, and that organised sex-trafficking networks use European and Gambian travel agencies to promote the country as a destination for it. Selling the trip as tourism is part of the method: it gives a buyer a reason to be in the country, a booking that looks like anyone else's, and a border crossing nobody queries. The same report says women and girls from other West African countries, especially Nigeria, are recruited with offers of jobs in tourism and then sexually exploited.

The Gambia legislated against this in 2003. Its Tourism Offences Act defines a child as anyone under 18, sets life imprisonment for child trafficking by tourists, and makes hotel operators liable if they knowingly allow child prostitution on their premises. Putting the duty on hotels is the most practical part of the law, because a hotel is licensed, has a fixed address, keeps a register and can be inspected. That is also the limit of what such a law can reach. By 2017 the US trafficking report found that traffickers in The Gambia were increasingly hosting child sex tourists in private residences outside the commercial tourist areas, where there is no licence to lose and no inspection to fail.

What the law could not touch at all was the demand, which lives in the countries the visitors fly from. Nor is there any measurement of the online side: no representative survey of technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation exists for West or Central Africa, so a shift from hotel rooms to webcams would not register in any figure for this country.

The Gambia is a short lesson in the limits of enforcement at the destination. Pressure applied to premises relocates the trade to places with no premises to regulate, which means the decisive question is what the buyer's own country does: whether it prosecutes its own citizens for sexual offences against children committed abroad.

LBN.mechanism: A raid that takes nobody's licence and brings no conviction leaves the business free to reopen, and a refugee population with no right to work keeps supplying it.
LBN.story:
Late in 2011, in the Maameltein district of Jounieh north of Beirut, Lebanese security forces raided a brothel called Chez Maurice and found a 17-year-old Syrian girl trapped inside. The place closed for about three months and then reopened. That interval is the whole mechanism: a raid removes the people found on the premises, but unless someone loses the building, the permission to operate it or their liberty, the business has only been interrupted.

In March 2016 the security forces raided Chez Maurice again, together with a second brothel called Silver-B, and freed as many as 75 Syrian women. More than a dozen people were arrested and indicted on sex-trafficking charges. A survivor told the Lebanese legal publication Legal Agenda that a trafficker had claimed he had bought the state. Lebanon's police identified 87 trafficking victims in the whole of 2016, almost all of them the people freed in that one operation, which is worth holding onto: a national figure can rest on a single raid, so it measures how often the police go in rather than how many people are held.

The women and girls came from the war next door. Human Rights Watch said Syrian refugee women were at particular risk, and the 2025 US trafficking report says criminal groups recruit Syrian women and girls with false offers of jobs and then exploit them in Lebanese brothels, while Syrian children are held in bonded labour in the Beqaa valley, meaning they work to pay off a debt that is calculated by the person holding them. A refugee with no legal right to work is dependent on whoever offers her something, and has no standing to complain about what it turns out to be.

Nothing is measured online. There is no representative survey of technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation anywhere in the Middle East and North Africa.

Lebanon shows that the test of a raid is what happens to the premises afterwards, not how many people were led out of it on the day. When a brothel where a child was found is trading again within months, the questions are who licensed it, who owns the building, and whether anyone was charged the first time.

MHL.mechanism: An adoption bought at both ends, with a payment to the mother, a larger fee from the adopters and a public official taking the difference.
MHL.story:
Between 2015 and 2019 recruiters working for Paul Petersen, an adoption lawyer who was also the elected assessor of Maricopa County in Arizona, found pregnant women in the Marshall Islands and arranged their travel to the United States. About 40 were flown to Arizona, Utah and Arkansas. Petersen paid each woman about $10,000 to give up her baby and charged the adopting American couples about $35,000.

The gap between those two figures is the business, and it is also the thing adoption law exists to prevent. Consent to give up a child is supposed to be free, because a mother who is being paid is not deciding whether she can raise her child but what the money is worth to her. Treaty rules were written with exactly this in mind: the Compact of Free Association, the agreement that governs relations between the Marshall Islands and the United States, lets Marshallese citizens travel freely to the US but specifically bars travel for the purpose of adoption, so that a poor mother cannot simply be brought to where the buyers are. Petersen also obtained about $814,000 in Arizona Medicaid funds by fraud for the women's medical care, which means the public paid the costs of running the scheme.

Complaints had begun by 2017. He was charged in October 2019 in Utah, Arizona and Arkansas, pleaded guilty in all three courts in June 2020 to human smuggling, fraud and communication fraud, and in December 2020 a federal court in Arkansas sentenced him to more than six years in prison.

This case is the clearest illustration on the map of how an adoption is bought: a payment at the poor end, a fee at the wealthy end, and someone with public authority arranging the paperwork in between. When an adoption crosses a border, the facts that settle whether it was lawful are who received money, how much, and whether the mother was allowed to travel for that purpose at all.

LBY.mechanism: The men who control a migration route can also sell the people on it, and a government that has never prosecuted anyone for trafficking is not a country without trafficking.
LBY.story:
In the desert towns of Ubari, Sabha and Murzuq in southern Libya, the 2025 US trafficking report says commercial sex rings hold women and girls from countries south of the Sahara in brothels, and that Nigerian women and girls are at increased risk. These are places on the route north: the towns where people who are trying to reach the Mediterranean have to stop, pay and wait. An international organisation cited in the report found that 77 per cent of children and young people passing through Libya showed indicators of exploitation amounting to trafficking.

Who holds those stopping points is the whole of it. The report says observers describe systemic complicity by officials, including members of the Libyan Coast Guard and immigration and security services. A migrant child in Libya has no legal status, and the authority that decides whether he is detained, released or sold is the same authority he would have to complain to.

The consequence is recorded plainly: the Libyan government has never reported prosecuting or convicting anyone for sex or labour trafficking. A prosecution needs a complainant who can safely come forward, an investigator who is not part of the trade and a court willing to hear it, and in Libya those three things do not currently line up. Nor is anything measured on the other side: there is no representative survey of technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation anywhere in the Middle East and North Africa.

Libya is the case to remember when a country shows no cases. Zero convictions can mean no crime, or it can mean that the people who would have to bring the case are the people the case would be against, and in a country where officials control the route, the second reading is the one the record supports. The question to ask of any such figure is who, concretely, would have had to file it.

YEM.mechanism: In a collapsed state the police and army are the largest single category in the verified count, which means the office a family would report to is the office responsible.
YEM.story:
UN monitors verified sexual violence against 24 children in Yemen during 2023, eight boys and 16 girls. Twenty of those cases were attributed to the Yemen Armed Forces and the forces aligned with them: nine to the army itself, four to the Yemeni police, and the rest to allied formations including the Security Belt and the Amaliqah. In 2024 they verified 11 cases, six boys and five girls, two attributed to the Houthi movement, two to the Yemen Armed Forces and seven to allied forces, four of those to the police.

Those numbers do two jobs. The first is to show where the risk sits. In a country at war, the forces that hold a town are also the only authority in it, and in Yemen's verified record the police and army account for more of the cases than the armed group they are fighting. There is no separate institution a parent can walk into. The second job is to show how little any figure like this can cover. To verify a case, a UN monitor has to confirm it, which in practice means reaching the child or a witness, in a country where front lines, checkpoints and the fear of reprisal stand between a monitor and almost everyone. Two dozen confirmed cases in a nation of millions is a statement about access, not about scale.

Beyond the war nothing has been measured at all. Childlight's 2026 update, which estimates how many children are abused online, rests on representative surveys from only 60 countries, and the Middle East and North Africa has none, so there is no figure of any kind for abuse in Yemen outside the conflict reports.

Yemen is where the counting problem and the perpetrator problem are the same problem: the institutions that would record complaints are implicated in them, and the only outside body that counts cannot reach most of the country. When a war-zone figure looks small, treat it as a measure of how far the monitors got.

PRY.mechanism: Distance is the protection: a man moved far enough from the complaints arrives with his standing intact, because no criminal record was ever created to travel with him.
PRY.story:
Fr Carlos Urrutigoity was accused of abuse in the Catholic Diocese of Scranton, in Pennsylvania, in 2002. He and the group of followers around him later moved to Ciudad del Este, in eastern Paraguay. He was not kept at a distance from authority there: in 2014 he was appointed vicar general, the bishop's deputy, a post with authority over the diocese's priests. In 2015 he was moved on again, to Mendoza in Argentina.

The reason a move like this works is that nothing portable was ever created. An accusation handled inside a church produces a file in a chancery office, not a charge, a conviction or an entry in any police system, so there is no record that follows the man across a border and nothing a receiving diocese can look up. It knows what the sending diocese chooses to tell it, and a transfer is normally accompanied by a recommendation rather than a warning.

The same distance serves people with no institution behind them. In April 2021 one of the German administrators of Boystown, a child abuse website taken down by European investigators, was found living in Paraguay and arrested there, which happened only because an international investigation had already identified him elsewhere.

Paraguay also appears on this map as a country children left. Between 1994 and 2003, United States immigrant visas were issued to 1,142 children adopted from Asunción, 483 of them in 1994 alone. The sources reached here record the numbers and no inquiry into how those placements were made, so the figures stand on their own.

Paraguay is the receiving end of the oldest move in these records, and the thing that makes it possible is the absence of a criminal case rather than the presence of a conspiracy. When a cleric or a teacher arrives from another country, the useful questions are why he left his last post, who in the new one was told, and whether any police force in either country ever had a file on him.

FJI.mechanism: The receiving end of a transfer: a small country far from the investigating police force, where an accused man arrives as a priest in good standing.
FJI.story:
In 1999 Australian police began investigating Julian Fox, a priest of the Salesian order. That year the order transferred him to Fiji. He was jailed in 2015.

Two separate things happen in a move like that, and it is worth keeping them apart. The first is practical: a police force's powers stop at its own border, so an investigation that was gathering statements in Australia had to start again through other countries' authorities, which takes years if it happens at all. The second is about reputation. A transferred priest does not arrive in Fiji under suspicion; he arrives with the order's appointment, and the people he will be working among know only what the order tells them. There was no conviction at that point and therefore nothing in any record that a parish could have consulted.

How often this happened is not established. In July 2020 the New Zealand broadcaster 1News reported about 1,300 alleged cases of child abuse by clergy in Fiji, said that some of them involved clergy from Australia and New Zealand, and quoted a survivor advocate saying Fiji was a common destination for clergy who had been transferred. The reports do not say how many of those 1,300 allegations concerned men sent from abroad, and this record does not fill that in.

Fiji is on the map because it was where men were sent, which is the half of these cases that usually goes unexamined; the attention falls on the diocese or order that moved someone, not on the community that received him. When a priest, teacher or doctor is posted abroad at the moment an investigation opens at home, ask who authorised the posting and what the receiving parish, school or clinic was told about him.

HKG.mechanism: Two unrelated roles: a law that follows a resident across the border to prosecute him at home, and a hosting industry that stores the material without the abuse happening there.
HKG.story:
Hong Kong passed the Prevention of Child Pornography Ordinance in December 2003. Among other things it gave 24 sexual offences what lawyers call extraterritorial effect. Criminal law normally stops at a border: a court tries offences committed in its own territory and nothing else. Extraterritorial effect removes that limit for particular crimes, so a Hong Kong resident can be tried at home for abusing a child in another country. This matters because the country where the abuse happens is often the one least able to prosecute, and a man who flies home has in practice left the case behind.

Hong Kong was one of several places to pass such a law in those years, after child sex tourism repeatedly moved rather than stopped. Observers reported that child prostitution in the Cambodian village of Svay Pak grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003, the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had already been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. When Manila closed its Ermita district in 1992, the businesses moved to Angeles City. Germany legislated in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003.

Hong Kong's larger presence in this record is as a storage address. The Internet Watch Foundation, which finds abuse images online and asks hosting companies to remove them, counted 24,063 web addresses hosted in Hong Kong across 2023 to 2025. The territory was the third or fourth largest host in the world in 2023 and 2024, and then its share fell sharply in 2025. Hosting figures describe where companies keep servers, which is a commercial decision about price, speed and how quickly a provider answers a removal notice, and says nothing about where a child was harmed.

Hong Kong is useful for showing that a place can hold two quite different positions in the same system, one legal and one commercial. When a country's hosting numbers drop steeply, the thing to check is whether the material was deleted or whether another country's numbers went up by about the same amount.

KAZ.mechanism: A sending country that has never been examined: the numbers of children who left exist, the inquiry into how they were obtained does not.
KAZ.story:
Between 2003 and 2022, 6,541 children were sent abroad from Kazakhstan for adoption, according to figures compiled by Selman. The United States alone issued immigrant visas to 6,612 children adopted from Astana between the 1994 and 2014 financial years, with the highest single year, 826 children, in 2004.

Those numbers describe a flow of children; they say nothing about how the children came to be available, and that is what distinguishes one sending country from another. Intercountry adoption rests on two documents: a paper establishing that the child has no family able to raise them, and a record of a parent's consent. When an inquiry opens, those two documents are what it examines, and in country after country it has found them false. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008, and its Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2025 that agencies had registered children with living, known parents as orphans and had not properly obtained consent. Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2007 and 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia, which banned foreign adoption in 2018, were each closed after inquiries found children bought, stolen or falsely recorded as orphans.

Receiving countries have begun to examine their own files for the same reason: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government commission reported, and China ended it in 2024.

No inquiry into Kazakhstan's adoptions appears in the sources reached, and the country is still sending children. That is the state of the record rather than a finding about it.

Kazakhstan is on this map as an open question rather than a proven case, and the reason it is worth marking is that every closed pipeline looked exactly like this before someone checked the paperwork. Where adoption from a country continues, the question is who verifies, for each child, that no family was able to keep them, and whether anyone has ever audited those verifications.

TLS.mechanism: An institution can act quickly on a complaint and still protect the accused, by keeping the penalty private so that nobody around him knows it exists.
TLS.story:
Allegations against Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo reached the Vatican in 2019. In 2020 the Vatican imposed sanctions on him. It did not say so. The matter became public only in 2022.

Church sanctions are restrictions imposed under the church's own law: limits on where a man may live, whom he may minister to, whether he may appear in public as a cleric. They are not a criminal penalty. No court is involved, no finding is published, and nobody outside the institution is told, which means the restrictions depend entirely on the man obeying them and on his superiors noticing if he does not. During those years the people he lived among, and the parents of any children he encountered, had no way of learning that his own church had judged the allegations serious enough to act on.

That is a different failure from the one that runs through most of this map. Across the 41 cases where the sources date both the first complaint that reached an authority and the first conviction, charge or official finding, the middle wait is 12 years, and many of the longest waits ran because nobody acted at all: a pupil told police about the MP Cyril Smith in 1968, and in 2012, two years after Smith's death, prosecutors said he should have been charged; complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known television presenters, reached police from 1958, and investigations in his lifetime brought no charges. Three years is fast by that standard. The Belo record shows that speed is not the same as disclosure, and that an institution can satisfy itself while leaving the public exactly where it was.

Timor-Leste is the case to hold in mind whenever an organisation announces that an allegation has been dealt with. The things that determine whether anyone was actually protected are what the penalty was, who was informed of it, whether anyone could check that it was being obeyed, and whether the police were ever told at all.

BEN.mechanism: A country with no measured figure, because the only method that finds unreported abuse, a representative survey, has never been run anywhere in its region.
BEN.story:
Most child sexual abuse is never reported to anyone, so counting police cases will always find a fraction of it. The method that finds the rest is a representative survey: researchers ask a sample of people, chosen so that their answers can stand for the whole population, whether these things happened to them. It is the only route to a number that includes the cases nobody ever took to an authority.

Childlight, a research centre that estimates how many children are sexually exploited and abused online, built its 2026 update on representative surveys from 60 countries. West and Central Africa is one of the regions with none, so no survey has ever asked the question in Benin, and the figure shown for it on this map is an estimate carried over rather than a measurement. A world total assembled from 60 countries also carries the shape of those 60: whatever is unusual about the places that have been surveyed is built into the global number, and whatever is unusual about Benin is not.

The other way a country enters international figures is by reporting its own police and court records. That route is nearly as thin. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 of them supplied data for 2023, and a government that does not answer the questionnaire simply does not appear.

Benin's place in this record is not a finding about children in Benin. It is a finding about who has done the asking: an empty country here marks the edge of the research, and the research has been funded and carried out largely elsewhere. When a map or a report shows a region as blank or low, the question is whether anyone has ever surveyed a population there, and when.

EGY.mechanism: The world's largest count of online abuse is a reporting line run in one country for its own technology companies, so the figures track which apps people use as much as where children are harmed.
EGY.story:
In 2025 the US CyberTipline received 23.4 million reports of suspected online child sexual exploitation. Fourteen per cent of them could not be placed in any country at all.

It is worth knowing what that line is before reading any number from it. The CyberTipline is an American reporting system, and the reports come from the technology companies themselves, nearly all of them American, passing on what they find on their own services. So a report exists when one of those companies notices something. A country where people use those platforms heavily generates many reports; a country where they do not generates few, whatever is happening to children there. Placing each report in a country then depends on tracing an internet address, which is why one report in seven in 2025 belonged nowhere. North Korea, where almost nobody can reach an American app, produced 12 reports that year. Nobody reads that as 12 incidents.

Egypt has no second source to correct the picture. Childlight, a research centre that estimates how many children are abused online, based its 2026 update on representative surveys, meaning surveys of a sample chosen to stand for a whole population, and it had them from only 60 countries; none of them covers the Middle East and North Africa. The route through governments is similarly incomplete: the UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023.

Egypt matters here as a lesson in how to read one of these global numbers. A reporting total measures the reporting system first and the harm second, and a country can be low on it because of which apps its people use, or because an internet address could not be traced. Before comparing two countries' figures, find out who was obliged to make the reports and what, exactly, triggered one.

TUN.mechanism: The main international count of trafficking is assembled from what governments choose to send in, so a country that does not answer is simply absent from it.
TUN.story:
The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries. Only 72 of them supplied figures for 2023.

The report does not count cases itself. It writes to governments and compiles what they return: the victims their officials identified, the suspects their police investigated, the convictions their courts recorded. Two different gaps follow from that. A government that does not reply leaves a blank, and a government that replies truthfully with nothing, because its police recorded no cases, produces a figure that looks like safety. Neither outcome has anything to do with how many children were harmed, which is why these returns cannot be compared country by country as though they were measurements.

Tunisia has no figure from the other route either. Childlight, a research centre that estimates how many children are sexually exploited online, bases its work on representative surveys, in which a sample of people chosen to stand for a whole population is asked directly about their own experience. Its 2026 update had such surveys from 60 countries, and none of them covers the Middle East and North Africa. Asking the population is the only method that reaches abuse nobody reported, and in Tunisia it has not been done.

So both doors are shut: nothing from a survey, and nothing a government has reported. The colour on this map for Tunisia is produced by estimate, and this is why.

Tunisia is an example of what an absence in international statistics actually consists of, which is an unanswered questionnaire and an unasked survey. When a figure is quoted for any country, the first thing to establish is which of the two it came from: a government's own return, or somebody asking the people who would know.

ARE.mechanism: Nothing has been measured, so a blank country reads as a safe one; the gap belongs to the measuring systems, not to the children.
ARE.story:
A reader who sees an empty country on a map of documented cases will take the obvious meaning from it. In the case of the United Arab Emirates the three systems that would have produced evidence can each be checked, and each of them stops short of the country.

The first is the direct one. Childlight, a research centre that estimates how many children are sexually exploited and abused online, works from representative surveys, which means asking a sample of people chosen so that their answers can stand for the whole population. Its 2026 update had such surveys from only 60 countries, and the Middle East and North Africa is one of the regions with none. Since most abuse is never reported to anyone, a survey is the only method that finds the unreported part, so where there is no survey there is no figure, only an estimate.

The second is the official one. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023; the report compiles what governments send in, so a government that does not answer leaves a blank that looks identical to a zero.

The third is the online reporting line, and it carries its own warning. In 2025 the US CyberTipline, which collects what technology companies, nearly all American, find on their own services, received 23.4 million reports; 14 per cent could not be traced to any country, and North Korea accounted for 12. A number that low records how few people there can reach an American platform.

The Emirates sit in this record as a demonstration that blank space on a map is a statement about research budgets, questionnaires and app usage. Before concluding anything from a country's absence, find out whether its children have ever been surveyed, whether its government answers the UN's request for figures, and which of those two a quoted number came from.
